name: Madhuvaneswarar Temple, Nannilam
deity: Shiva as Madhuvaneswarar (lord of the honey-forest), with the goddess Madhuvana Nayaki
tradition: Shaiva — a Paadal Petra Sthalam, sung by Appar and Sundarar
period: Tevaram era; traditionally a Kochengat Chola Maada Kovil
summary: Nannilam honours Shiva as Madhuvaneswarar — lord of the honey-forest — with the goddess Madhuvana Nayaki, a Paadal Petra Sthalam praised by Appar and sung by Sundarar in nine verses, who called the great temple of Nannilam by its name. A self-manifested lingam set in a once-forested place of madhu trees, it is counted among the raised Maada Kovils traditionally built by the Chola king Kochengat Chola, and remembered in legend as a refuge of the gods.

sections.history: Nannilam, a town in the delta country, is an ancient Shaiva site hymned in the seventh-century Tevaram — praised by Appar and sung by Sundarar in nine verses, whose closing lines name the Chola king as its builder. The temple is held to be one of the raised Maada Kovils traditionally ascribed to Kochengat Chola, built high so that an elephant could not enter the sanctum. Sundarar's name for it, Nannilathu Perunkovil, the great temple of Nannilam, marks its standing in the delta.
sections.architecture: As a Maada Kovil the temple sits on an elevated base in the manner of the Kochengat Chola foundations. The sanctum enshrines the self-manifested lingam of Madhuvaneswarar; the goddess Madhuvana Nayaki has her own shrine. The temple's name, from a forest of madhu trees, and its honey-bee legend give its iconography and worship a distinctive flavour among the delta shrines.
sections.legends: The name Madhuvaneswarar comes from a forest of madhu trees that once surrounded the shrine. One tradition tells that in the Dvapara age, when the asura Vrithrasura tormented the gods, they prayed to Shiva, who turned the Devas into honeybees and let them dwell in the sanctum to worship the lingam — from which the lord takes the name of the honey-forest. Another account calls the place Devaranyam, the gods' forest, where the Devas sheltered from the asura Jalandhara, whom Shiva vanquished at nearby Virkudi. The self-manifested lingam and the god's own name keep these stories alive.
sections.festivals: The temple keeps the Shaiva festival calendar — Maha Shivaratri, Pradosham, the Margazhi season and the annual Brahmotsavam. Its standing as the 'great temple of Nannilam' and its Maada Kovil form give the festivals of the delta town a focus here, and Sundarar's hymn is cherished in the temple's tradition.
sections.experience: Nannilam offers the pilgrim a raised temple with a gentle legend at its heart — gods made into bees to worship the lingam in a forest of honey. Climbing to the elevated sanctum of Madhuvaneswarar, and standing before a self-manifested lord sung by Appar and Sundarar, the visitor meets a shrine whose sweetness is woven into its very name.

visit.timings: Typically open from early morning to midday and again from late afternoon into the evening; confirm timings locally, especially on festival days.
visit.dressCode: Modest traditional attire is expected, with shoulders and knees covered; footwear is left at the entrance.
visit.photography: Photography is generally allowed in the outer corridors but not inside the sanctum; ask temple staff before photographing rituals.
visit.gettingThere: Nannilam is a town in Tiruvarur district, about 17 km from Tiruvarur; it has its own railway station and is well connected by bus from Tiruvarur, Nagapattinam and Kumbakonam.
